source: Sherbino et al. (2014) Ineffectiveness of cognitive forcing strategies to reduce biases in diagnostic reasoning: a controlled trial
finding: First experimental test of cognitive forcing strategy (CFS) training. Trained students did no better than controls on cases built to trigger search satisficing or availability bias.
numbers: N=191 EM-rotation students (145 CFS, 46 control). Second diagnosis found: 54% vs 48% (p=0.13). Search for 2nd diagnosis started: 52% vs 48% (p=0.91). Uncommon correct diagnosis in availability cases: 45% vs 45% (p=0.98). False-positive oversearching cases: 64% vs 77% wrong (p=0.12).
limits: Abstract only read. Novices; one 4-week rotation; computer cases; control group small (46). Training may be too light to become automatic.
agent_relevance: Telling a model to be aware of a bias is the human analogue of this null result. Do not count on a generic beware-of-X line; add concrete steps or knowledge.

source: Norman et al. (2014) The etiology of diagnostic errors: a controlled trial of system 1 versus system 2 reasoning
finding: Instruction to be slow, careful and reflective did not raise accuracy over instruction to be fast. It only cost time.
numbers: N=204 second-year residents (96 Speed in 2010, 108 Reflect in 2011), 20 computer internal-medicine cases. Accuracy 44.5% Speed vs 45.0% Reflect (ns). Time 69 s vs 89 s per case (p<.001). Wrong cases took about 17 s longer than right ones in both groups.
limits: Abstract only read. Different cohorts in different years, not random assignment. Residents tested just after an exam. Time was inversely correlated with accuracy: hard cases are slow, so slowing is not the cure.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence against a slow-down or think-longer line. A pause with no new operation adds cost, not accuracy.

source: Norman et al. (2017) The causes of errors in clinical reasoning: cognitive biases, knowledge deficits, and dual process thinking
finding: Review: both Type 1 and Type 2 processes produce errors. Bias-recognition teaching does not cut errors; knowledge reorganisation gives small but consistent gains.
numbers: No pooled effect size. Key statement: induced biases (especially availability) are easy to show in the lab, but their share of real diagnostic error is not well established.
quote: Educational strategies directed at the recognition of biases are ineffective in reducing errors
limits: Abstract only read. Narrative, not systematic. Authors are the main proponents of the knowledge-deficit view, so rival-camp bias is possible.
agent_relevance: Supports the SCHEMA stance: add relevant knowledge and checks, not exhortations. Knowledge deficits may matter more than bias for our agent too.

source: Croskerry, Singhal, Mamede (2013) Cognitive debiasing 1: origins of bias and theory of debiasing
finding: Theory paper. Says evidence for bias as a cause of real diagnostic error is still scarce and borrowed from other domains. Debiasing is hard because bias is largely unconscious.
numbers: No data. Text says the evidence base is scarce and that findings come from other domains.
limits: Conceptual, opinion-heavy. This is the founding statement that later trials tested and mostly failed to confirm.
agent_relevance: Origin of the forcing-function idea. Treat as hypothesis, not result.

source: Croskerry, Singhal, Mamede (2013) Cognitive debiasing 2: impediments to and strategies for change
finding: Lists debiasing tools with evidence tags. States that cognitive forcing strategies showed minor effects and consider-the-opposite marginally reduced anchoring. Checklist support comes mostly from surgery and ICU, not diagnosis. Stopping rules: no published examples.
numbers: Surgical safety checklist and five-item line-infection checklist cited as successes (other domains). Anchoring consider-the-opposite: marginal. CFS: minor effects. Stopping rules: none published.
quote: Investigations on their effectiveness have not been so frequent and, presently, cognitive debiasing is an inexact science.
limits: Authors admit debiasing is an inexact science; many items rest on opinion.
agent_relevance: Even the proponents rate most items as weak. Stopping rules for enough thinking have no human evidence at all, so our exit rules are untested.

source: Ely, Graber, Croskerry (2011) Checklists to reduce diagnostic errors
finding: Proposes three checklist types: general cognitive, differential-diagnosis, and disease-specific pitfalls with forcing functions. Says they were developed informally and not rigorously evaluated.
numbers: No data. Explicit statement that the checklists have not been subjected to rigorous evaluation.
limits: Abstract only read. Proposal paper.
agent_relevance: Source of the checklist idea; shows the checklist route started as untested theory.

source: Sibbald et al. (2013) Checklists improve experts' diagnostic decisions
finding: Experts reading ECGs made fewer errors when a checklist was used at the verification stage, not at first interpretation. No rise in cognitive load, no expertise reversal.
numbers: N=15 experts, 18 ECGs, 4 conditions. Errors corrected in verification: 0.29 vs 0.03 per ECG. Net errors: 0.39 vs 1.04 per ECG (p<0.01 both). Cognitive load 3.7 vs 3.3 (ns). Checklists made reading longer (p<0.01).
limits: Abstract only read. Tiny sample, ECG only, a content-specific checklist, not a debiasing list.
agent_relevance: Best positive human signal fits our design: apply the checklist after the first answer (verification) and keep the first pass intact.

source: Sibbald et al. (2019) Debiasing versus knowledge retrieval checklists to reduce diagnostic error in ECG interpretation
finding: Neither a debiasing checklist nor a knowledge checklist beat control, even when half the ECGs were built to induce bias.
numbers: N=61 (40 PGY1 EM/IM residents, 21 cardiology fellows PGY4-6), 20 ECGs, 3 arms. No checklist effect vs control. Bias-built ECGs gave more errors (F=96.9, p<0.0001). No interaction with learner level; authors say checklists may help novices.
quote: Even when cognitive biases are deliberately inserted in cases, cognitive debiasing checklists did not improve participants' performance.
limits: Abstract only read. Small cells. Same research area found a benefit in 2013 with a verification-stage content list.
agent_relevance: Replication gap: a bias-naming list failed when bias was deliberately planted. A debiasing checklist should not be our main safeguard.

source: Jenkins and Youngstrom (2016) A randomized controlled trial of cognitive debiasing improves assessment and treatment selection for pediatric bipolar disorder
finding: A brief web debiasing course (pitfalls plus mnemonics and Bayesian tools) cut errors in mental-health vignettes.
numbers: N=137 mental-health professionals, 4 vignettes, random to PBD overview alone or overview plus debiasing. Treatment group had better accuracy and fewer errors (both p<.001). Patient race effect negligible.
limits: Abstract only read. Vignettes, one disorder, judgment on text. Taught concrete tools (Bayesian aids), not only warnings. Not general medicine.
agent_relevance: Positive result came with specific tools (base rates), which matches adding knowledge or operators over be-aware lines.

source: Smith and Slack (2015) The effect of cognitive debiasing training among family medicine residents
finding: A debiasing workshop changed little in real clinic visits.
numbers: Preceptor agreement with resident diagnosis 74% (63/85) vs 78% (45/58), p=0.64. Resident saw own bias risk: 51% vs 57% (p=0.46). Acceptable mitigation plan: 84% (36/43) to 100% (33/33), p=0.02. Unrecognised bias seen by preceptor: 12% vs 9% (p=0.55).
limits: Abstract only read. Pre-post, no control; outcomes are preceptor ratings, not patient outcomes. Only the plan outcome moved, which is easy to say.
agent_relevance: Learners can write a mitigation plan without detecting the bias. Words about debiasing are cheap; measure behaviour.

source: Costa Filho et al. (2019) Effects of deliberate reflection on diagnostic accuracy, confidence and diagnostic calibration in dermatology
finding: Structured reflection raised accuracy on dermatology images but left confidence and calibration unchanged.
numbers: N=61 sixth-year students, 12 images, reflection group vs filler. Accuracy 49.7 +/- 12.1 vs 38.4 +/- 14.6 (p=0.002). Confidence 64.3 vs 58.9 (p=0.228). Calibration gap 0.15 vs 0.20 (p=0.197). Overconfidence larger on hard cases (p<0.001).
quote: Deliberate reflection increased diagnostic accuracy in dermatology but did not affect confidence and calibration.
limits: Quasi-experimental: whole rotations allocated alternately, not individual randomisation. Visual task. Reflection took 3.5 min per case against 30 s for the first guess.
agent_relevance: Reflection can fix answers without fixing confidence, so a verifier must not trust the model's own confidence after reflecting. Link to the calibration subfield.

source: Guided reflection interventions show no effect on diagnostic accuracy in medical students (2018, Front Psychol)
finding: Failed replication of deliberate reflection with novices. Listing two or six alternative diagnoses did not beat first impressions on strict scoring.
numbers: N=186 fourth/fifth-year students. Strict accuracy: control 0.47, short (2 alternatives) 0.42, long (6 alternatives) 0.41. Lenient (right diagnosis anywhere in list): 0.70 and 0.72. Confidence did not change; rate of corrected diagnoses did not differ.
quote: This study finds no evidence to support the use of the guided reflection method as a diagnostic aid for novice diagnosticians
limits: Fictional cases. Lenient score inflates by list length. Authors suggest novices already reason analytically, so there is no room to gain. Conflicts with Mamede 2008/2010 and Myung 2013.
agent_relevance: Listing alternatives raises coverage but not final-choice accuracy. If our agent writes a differential, its final pick still needs an evidence-based selection step.

source: Mamede et al. (2020) Immunising physicians against availability bias in diagnostic reasoning: a randomised controlled experiment
finding: Increasing knowledge of how look-alike diseases differ protected residents from an induced availability bias. Process-only methods had largely failed before.
numbers: N=91 second-year IM residents, 8 hospitals, 3-phase design. On biased vignettes immunised 0.40 vs 0.24 (diff 0.16, 95% CI 0.05-0.27, p=0.004). On non-biased vignettes 0.36 vs 0.41 (p=0.45). Non-immunised fell 0.17 when biased (p=0.005); immunised did not (p=0.56).
limits: Simulated vignettes, one-week gap, two disease clusters (IBD/diarrhoea, hepatitis/jaundice). Unclear it generalises to other clusters.
agent_relevance: Strongest human case for knowledge-based debiasing: contrast sets of look-alike diagnoses, with feedback, before the case. Fits an operator that pulls discriminating features.

source: Mamede et al. (2012) Reflection as a strategy to foster medical students' acquisition of diagnostic competence
finding: Structured reflection during practice hurt performance at once but helped a week later, so the gain is in learning, not in the first answer.
numbers: N=46 Year-4 students. Immediate test: reflection 0.48 vs differential 0.62 (p=0.012) and immediate 0.61. Delayed test one week later: reflection 0.66 vs 0.48 and 0.52 (p<0.01 and p=0.01).
limits: Abstract only read. Small N, one lab.
agent_relevance: Reflection may build knowledge rather than catch errors. For a no-training agent, in-context reflection cannot give this delayed benefit.

source: Mamede et al. (2012) Exploring the role of salient distracting clinical features in diagnostic errors and how reflection counteracts mistakes
finding: Reflection helped residents by overriding salient but irrelevant features. Students did not benefit.
numbers: Secondary analysis of 34 residents and 50 students. Residents correct: reflective 2.09 vs non-analytic 1.71 (p=0.03). Errors from distractors: 0.47 vs 0.85 (p=0.02). Students: no benefit.
limits: Abstract only read. Secondary analysis of earlier data. Moderator is knowledge: reflection works only when the person can tell which features discriminate.
agent_relevance: Expertise moderator: a weak model may not gain from self-reflection. Test reflection separately per model strength.

source: Mamede (2023) Deliberate reflection and clinical reasoning: founding ideas and empirical findings
finding: Review from the lead lab. Reflection helps on complex cases and with residents; not on simple cases. Mechanism unclear. Notes that only 23 adequately controlled studies existed in the earlier Prakash review.
numbers: Early study: residents' accuracy improved by more than 35% with deliberate reflection on complex cases, no change on simple ones. Pattern reversed for students: better on simple cases, worse on complex ones. Transfer to look-alike disease seen in one study.
limits: Written by proponents. Lab vignettes, mostly one research network.
agent_relevance: Case-complexity moderator: apply the extra check when the case is hard or the first answer is weakly supported, not always.

source: Staal et al. (2022) Effect on diagnostic accuracy of cognitive reasoning tools for the workplace setting: systematic review and meta-analysis
finding: Meta-analysis of tools used at work (checklists, decision support, instructions at test, guided reflection) found a small gain.
numbers: 29 studies, 2732 participants. Pooled g=0.28 (95% CI 0.14-0.43), I2=70%. Without 3 studies that trained people first: g=0.20 (0.10-0.29), I2=38%. No moderator found by expertise, tool type, timing or items. Task type did: real/simulated patients 0.41 (0.33-0.49) vs visual or written. Egger p=0.077. Only 1 study preregistered.
limits: Only 2 studies used patients. Mostly small lab studies. Merges content-specific and process tools, so it cannot say that be-aware-of-bias works.
agent_relevance: Realistic ceiling for scaffolding of this kind is about 0.2 SD. Plan for small gains and measure them.

source: Systematic review of diagnostic checklists with a human-factors framework (2022)
finding: Of 14 checklists tested for effect, 7 helped, 6 did not, 1 mixed. Task-focused lists worked more often than cognitive-process lists.
numbers: 30 articles, 25 unique checklists. Task-oriented studies reduced errors in 5/7; cognitive-process ones in 4/10.
limits: Counts of studies, no pooled effect; vote counting; mixed quality.
agent_relevance: Prefer checklists that list concrete tasks (check this finding, rule out that diagnosis) over lists about thinking style.

source: Strategies to reduce diagnostic errors: a systematic review of audit and communication interventions (2019)
finding: Only real-patient interventions: trigger algorithms, extra review and team meetings had some evidence. Cognitive debiasing was not in this evidence set.
numbers: 2431 articles screened, 26 studies; 9 RCTs. 3 communication RCTs and 3 audit RCTs reported reduced diagnostic error. 73% of studies from the US.
limits: Scope is audit and communication, so the absence of debiasing here is by design.
agent_relevance: External review beats self-review: a second reader or trigger rule has more field evidence than an introspective pause.

source: Review of the basics of cognitive error in emergency medicine: still no easy answers (2020)
finding: Summarises slow-down trials: slowing raised time but not accuracy; slow conditions without interruptions did not help; slow-down on bias-inducing vignettes in an RCT of trainees and faculty did not help. Consider-the-opposite evidence for clinical reasoning is limited.
numbers: Cites Norman (more time, no accuracy gain), a trial of EPs and residents (no gain), an RCT of trainees and faculty (no gain). Jenkins positive; Sherbino and Smith-Slack null.
quote: Thus, while it may seem prudent to slow down when the physician does not know an answer, this strategy has not yet proven to be effective.
limits: Narrative review. Notes studies are small, single-centre, mostly students or residents, mostly lab.
agent_relevance: Cross-checks the null for slow down. Keep it out of the schema as a stand-alone step.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) Evaluation and mitigation of cognitive biases in medical language models
finding: BiasMedQA: 1273 USMLE questions rewritten to inject 7 clinical biases. Bias drops accuracy for most models; GPT-4 is most resilient. Three prompt fixes (bias warning, one-shot, few-shot) help but do not restore accuracy.
numbers: 6 LLMs. Least harmful bias was confirmation: -8.1% average (p<1e-16); other biases larger. Education (warning text) gave +3.5% to +6.5% for all models except PMC-Llama-13B (-0.1%, p=0.875). GPT-4 few-shot average accuracy 75.2%. GPT-3.5 education +6.1%, one-shot +4.3%, few-shot +5.2%. Llama-2-70B few-shot: -4.1% vs unmitigated. Education on cultural bias lowered scores for Mixtral (-3.0%), GPT-3.5 (-0.3%), PMC-Llama (-2.2%), none significant.
limits: Biases are injected by a sentence in an exam question, not natural. Medical QA, not open diagnosis. Older models. Warning text is tailored to each bias.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM analogue of bias awareness. A warning line gives small gains (about 3-6 points) and never fully repairs. Few-shot negative examples can backfire on weak models.

source: Ke et al. (2024) Mitigating cognitive biases in clinical decision-making through multi-agent conversations using large language models
finding: Role-based GPT-4 agents (devil's advocate, facilitator, expert, recorder) fixed misdiagnoses in cases built from reports of bias-driven errors.
numbers: 16 case reports, 5 repeats each. Initial diagnosis 0/80 correct by design. After discussion top-2 diagnoses: 3-agent 51/80 (64%, OR 1.91, p=.10), 4-agent 55/80 (69%, OR 2.39, p=.03), 4-agent with explicit bias discussion (4-C) 61/80 (76%, OR 3.49, p=.002). Humans 13/48 (27%) initial, 23/48 (48%) final. A 5th agent did not take part.
limits: Cases chosen because the first diagnosis was wrong, so the starting 0% is selection. Comparison group small (48) and answers differ in format (top-2). No control without agents; text only; GPT-4 pretraining may include the case reports.
agent_relevance: Strongest positive LLM signal for a devil's advocate role, but the gain from naming bias (4-C vs 4) is small (69% to 76%) and untested without agents. Run an ablation of our own.

source: Wang and Redelmeier (2024) Cognitive biases and artificial intelligence (NEJM AI)
finding: GPT-4 and Gemini-1.0-Pro show human-like biases in 10 clinical vignette pairs, often larger than in clinicians.
numbers: Framing: surgery recommended 75% vs 12% (p<0.001). Primacy: pulmonary embolism listed 100% vs 26% (p<0.001). Hindsight: 85% vs 0% (p<0.001). Base-rate neglect showed none: 94% vs 93% (p=0.431). Synthetic-clinician prompts changed bias little.
limits: Abstract only read. Older models; vignette pairs.
agent_relevance: The order of presented facts changes the differential. Our agent should compare answers under reordered inputs (a cheap consistency check).

source: Degany, Laros, Idan, Einav (2025) Evaluating the o1 reasoning large language model for cognitive bias: a vignette study
finding: A reasoning model with built-in step-by-step thinking showed less bias than GPT-4 but not none, and was worse on one vignette.
numbers: 10 vignette pairs (Wang and Redelmeier method), 90 outputs per version, 1,800 responses. No measurable bias in 7 of 10. Significant but smaller than GPT-4 or clinicians in 2. Consistent bias in Occam's razor. Intra-scenario agreement above 94%. More bias when a gap-closing cue removed uncertainty.
limits: Vignettes, one model and date (o1-2024-12-17). Comparison with GPT-4 uses published numbers, not a same-time run.
agent_relevance: Extra reasoning compute lowers bias and noise but not to zero; a cue that seems to close the question is the danger point, like premature closure.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley, He (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: On student-admission decisions (not medical), awareness prompts gave small gains, few-shot examples sometimes broke the model, and letting the model rewrite its own prompt to remove bias worked best.
numbers: GPT-4 admits 40.5% more students under the reject framing. Llama-2-7B: 32.1% fewer females judged good at math. Self-help rewrite left biased prompt elements at 0% for group attribution (GPT-4), 2.7% framing. Llama models changed 40-52% of decisions in the self-help setup. Few-shot sometimes drove answers to probability 0 or 1.
limits: Admissions, not medicine. Small open models behave differently from GPT-4: self-debiasing only worked for high-capacity models.
agent_relevance: Self-help means the model first strips bias-laden framing from the input, then decides. A cheap pre-step; benefit depends on model size.

source: Bucinca, Malaya, Gajos (2021) To trust or to think: cognitive forcing functions can reduce overreliance on AI in AI-assisted decision-making
finding: Forcing people to think first (or wait) before seeing AI advice cut overreliance on wrong AI advice, at the cost of liking and trust. It did not remove overreliance.
numbers: N=199 MTurk workers, 6 conditions in a nutrition task. Forcing functions reduced overreliance more than simple explanations. Benefit larger for high Need-for-Cognition people. Participants preferred the designs that worked least.
limits: Lay people on a food task, simulated AI. Strong individual difference: forcing helps motivated thinkers most.
agent_relevance: Same logic for an agent: commit to its own answer before seeing a tool or critic output. An independent-first rule guards against anchoring on critics.

source: Independent judgment before viewing generative AI recommendations (2026, randomised scenario experiment with preservice teachers)
finding: Recording own judgment before seeing AI advice reduced acceptance of misleading AI advice and did not hurt with good advice.
numbers: N=240 preservice teachers (218 analysed). Under misleading advice: OR 1.912 (95% CI 1.413-2.589, p<0.001) for accuracy favouring independent-first. Reproduced misleading advice less: OR 0.403 (0.296-0.549). Expert-keyed advice: OR 0.821 (p=0.225, ns).
limits: Abstract only read. Education not medicine, one Chinese university, one scenario set.
agent_relevance: Independent-first is a pattern across domains (see Bucinca). Supports ordering steps so the agent commits before consulting.

source: AI Timeouts: A Structured Approach to Deliberate AI Use in Clinician Education (2026)
finding: Proposes two structured pauses (before and after AI use) borrowed from the procedural timeout and cognitive forcing strategies.
numbers: No data; framework only.
limits: Abstract only read. No test.
agent_relevance: Shows the idea is spreading from human CFS into AI use without new outcome evidence.
